sentences.text: Thalattosuchus measured between 3 and 4.5 meters in length, a size similar to modern crocodiles.
This marine reptile possessed nasal salt glands used to remove excess salt from its body.
Because it lost the osteoderms, or bony shields, characteristic of other crocodiles, it likely had few natural defenses against larger marine predators.
Although the genus Thalattosuchus was named in 2020, its fossils were historically classified under the species Metriorhynchus superciliosus.
Fossil specimens are known from Middle to Late Jurassic deposits in England, France, and Germany.
Thalattosuchus was a versatile and opportunistic predator that hunted armored belemnites, fast and elusive fish, and larger species like the filter-feeding fish Leedsichthys.
It occasionally attempted to capture flying animals like pterosaurs and fed on plesiosaur carcasses on the sea floor.
Despite being an effective predator, Thalattosuchus was vulnerable to larger predators like the 10-meter-long pliosaur Liopleurodon.
Pellarin et al. (2026) suggest that exceptionally well-developed frontoparietal fossae in the skull of T. superciliosus may be an adaptation for surface basking to facilitate cranial heat transfer.
The genus Thalattosuchus was established by Young et al. in 2020 after a cladistic analysis showed it should be separated from Metriorhynchus.
Thalattosuchus lived from the Callovian to the Kimmeridgian stages, approximately 165.3 to 149.2 million years ago.
Not all researchers accept the split; in 2022, a team led by Jonas le Mort proposed synonymizing Thalattosuchus back into Metriorhynchus.
